did_you_know.text: The psalm opens with a unique title: “A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day”—presenting itself as a song intended for the Sabbath.
The psalmist presents giving thanks to the Lord and singing praises to His name as good and fitting: “It is good to give thanks to the Lord and to sing praises to Your name, Most High.”
Praise for the Lord continues throughout the day and night: His loving-kindness is proclaimed in the morning, and faithfulness is expressed at night.
The psalm mentions several musical instruments accompanying the singing: the ten-stringed instrument, the harp, and the lyre, along with the musical melody or accompaniment played on them.
The psalmist describes personal joy in the Lord’s works and emphasizes that God’s deeds are great and His thoughts profound.
According to the psalm, a foolish person does not understand the meaning of the wicked’s temporary flourishing or the fate that awaits them.
The wicked are compared to grass that grows quickly: they may flourish for a short time, but the psalm declares that their end is destruction, unlike the Lord, who is eternal.
The psalmist uses the images of a raised wild ox’s horn and fresh oil to portray exaltation, strength, and renewal.
The righteous are compared to a date palm and a cedar: the palm that flourishes and the cedar of Lebanon that grows with strength and stability.
The psalm emphasizes that even in old age, the righteous continue to bear fruit, remain full of sap, and stay fresh—testifying to their enduring vitality.
